chunks: "Impedance matching means making the impedances at a junction line up so the signal passes through without bouncing back.

On a transmission line that means the source impedance, the line's characteristic impedance and the load impedance are all the same, say 50 ohms, so the reflection coefficient is zero at both ends and the wave goes from driver to receiver exactly once.

In RF it also gives maximum power transfer: with a source resistance R S the load gets the most power when R L equals R S , half of the source power, and for reactive sources you match to the complex conjugate.
I care because without it you get reflections: overshoot, ringing, false edges and eye closure on digital signals, and standing waves, lost power and instability in RF.
When to use it: whenever the line is electrically long compared with the signal edge, roughly when the one-way delay is more than a sixth of the rise time.
So for fast clocks, DDR, USB or PCIe, any RF path, and long cables.

When not to: short traces and slow signals, where a termination would only burn power and slow the edge, and power distribution, where you want a low source impedance and a high load impedance rather than a match."
